A few days ago I was sitting on the floor, and suddenly the thought came in my head after feeling something rubbing on my skin. I've tried weeks prior to see if my skin and brain can actually determine an absolute location based on the sensations (this wall feels 2 meters away), or just an illusive relative location (this wall is on my finger which I assume is 2 meters away).

I decided it was a relative thing, which made more sense. Fast forward back to a few days ago and I got this thought.. where is "me"? Was I actually just a point of consciousness like I've heard in philosophies before, or just a collection of senses? After all, the only reason we see out of our heads is because our eyes are there, and only reason we hear from our heads is because our ears are there. If our eyes were on our feet then we would be seeing from our feet, and likewise with our ears, and sense of smell. The only reason things feel and sound closer to our heads is because of the senses of touch and hearing working together to perceive direction and distance, so I figure the same would be true if our eyes and ears were in a different place.

So is it possible that we are not in our bodies, just receiving its sensory information? If so, where are we? Is there even a "where" in this sense? Could we actually be in some control room in another dimension receiving outputs from our body? Could we have no location at all?
Your point of consciousness is not in your head.

I've entertained the notion that "I" (the Observer) is in another, connected dimension. Another thought-provoking question, if you accept the extra-dimensional approach, is "When am I?" As in, is my experience of linear time an artifact of the senses I am connected to in the physical realm and, if so, is it possible that "I" (in my non-physical dimension) am capable of non-linear time perception?

I, too, have these thoughts in the shower.

I would assume that our consciousness would have to be either in the same time or slightly behind the body in time, because it would have to accept a continuous stream of input from the body, and the body a continuous stream of commands. Inputs may last from the past but that's due to sensations still firing off in the present, and the future isn't possible to feel.

But perhaps the less involved the body is with consciousness, the faster time goes, and vice versa. This could be explained through sleep (lack of body sensations reaching consciousness), and adrenaline (the opposite). Hmm.
No. We're just a series of very complicated neurons that fire when receiving specific stimulus from external sources.
